Menu Costs: When Prices Won't Move

In micro, an out-of-place price moved at once. In macro, the cost of changing price tags holds prices still.

Changing a price means reprinting the menu. Shops hate that cost, so they put up with small losses. Only a shock past the threshold below makes them move. While prices stay frozen, sales and jobs take the hit instead.

For example, ✏️ pencils at the 🏪 stationery shop cost 500 won. Costs creep up a little, but the owner leaves the tag alone. Rewriting every tag is more trouble than the small loss. Instead, the shop simply stocks fewer pencils.

π(p)=π∗−k(p−p∗)2\pi(p) = \pi^* - k(p - p^*)^2π(p)=π∗−k(p−p∗)2
δ∗=F/k\delta^* = \sqrt{F / k}δ∗=F/k​

Examples & Exercises

The market's ideal price fell by 111.

A restaurant with a menu cost of 444 — does it reprint its price list? (Standing still loses 2δ22\delta^22δ2.)

Show proof

  1. Standing still loses 2⋅12=22 \cdot 1^2 = 22⋅12=2. That is less than the menu cost 444, so reprinting would lose more than it saves — the rational choice is to leave the price alone.

    Profit is 100−2=98100 - 2 = 98100−2=98, nearly intact: near the top of the profit hill the ground is flat, so a small miss barely hurts.

  2. Quantity absorbs it instead: the now-too-high price sheds 555 customers, and volume falls from 505050 to 454545. The price is spotless while the quantity is bruised — the face of a short-run macro fluctuation.

    (The band's edge is 4/2≈1.41\sqrt{4 / 2} \approx 1.414/2​≈1.41: any smaller shock is swallowed whole.)

This time the ideal price fell by 333.

What does the same restaurant, menu cost 444, do now?

Show proof

  1. The loss grows with the square: 2⋅32=182 \cdot 3^2 = 182⋅32=18. Triple the shock, nine times the loss.

    That towers over the menu cost 444, so cutting the price wins. After adjusting, profit is 100−4=96100 - 4 = 96100−4=96, far better than the 100−18=82100 - 18 = 82100−18=82 from standing still.

  2. The price moved from 101010 to 777, so volume recovers to 505050. Big shocks are absorbed by prices and leave quantities whole; small shocks are absorbed by quantities and leave prices whole — which side takes the hit depends on the shock's size.
